title: ITA Section 37(1.3): SR&ED Repayments & EEZ Legislation
description: Examine Canada's ITA Section 37(1.3) legislation covering SR&ED repayments and research expenditures within Canada's exclusive economic zone.
summary: For Canadian businesses assessing how assistance and repayments affect SR&ED claims under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, government and non-government assistance, including NRC IRAP grants and provincial R&D tax credits, reduces the deductible SR&ED pool and qualified expenditures before the federal 35% or 15% investment tax credit is calculated, and claims must be filed within 18 months.

Executive Legal and Fiscal Architecture of the Canadian R&D Regime

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework is anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program, which operates alongside an intricate network of provincial and territorial tax credits, accelerated capital cost allowances, and direct innovation grants. Administered jointly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the Department of Finance Canada, the SR&ED program represents the single largest federal expenditure supporting business innovation in the country. Rather than functioning as a discretionary subsidy, the federal SR&ED regime is a statutory entitlement codified within the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Any taxpayer carrying on business in Canada that executes qualifying scientific or technological investigation within the statutory meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and files the prescribed disclosures within the statutory reporting window, is legally entitled to both an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable income deduction under section 37 and an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under section 127.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most profound legislative and administrative transformation in over a decade. At the federal level, following extensive two-phase policy consultations initiated in early 2024, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, cited as the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds to a $15 million to $75 million corridor, extended the enhanced 35% credit to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of depreciable capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE). Concurrently, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA introduced an elective pre-claim approval mechanism that halves expenditure review timelines from 180 days to 90 days. At the provincial level, Quebec executed a structural overhaul effective for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing five legacy R&D tax credits—including the longstanding tax credit for R&D salaries and wages—and consolidating support into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

Empirical fiscal data released in 2026 by the Department of Finance Canada and the CRA illustrates the expanding macroeconomic footprint of the federal SR&ED program. In the Report on Federal Tax Expenditures 2026 (Part 2), the Department of Finance estimated the annual federal fiscal cost of the SR&ED investment tax credit at $5,176 million ($5.176 billion) for the 2025 calendar year. Over the four-year period spanning fiscal year 2021/22 to fiscal year 2025/26 (where CRA fiscal years run from April 1 to March 31), the annual volume of SR&ED claims submitted to the CRA increased by 18.8%, rising from 20,332 claims in 2021/22 to 24,160 claims in 2025/26. Over the same interval, aggregate SR&ED ITCs claimed surged by 44.1%, expanding from $3.4 billion to $4.9 billion, of which the CRA allowed $4.6 billion in 2025/26. Consequently, the average SR&ED claim size rose from approximately $167,000 in 2021/22 to $203,000 in 2025/26.

body.text: A granular examination of the 2025/26 CRA statistical cohort reveals a pronounced structural bifurcation between claim volume and credit value, as well as a rapid concentration of tax expenditures within the digital economy. Small businesses accounted for 65% of all processed SR&ED claims in 2025/26 but captured only 33% of total ITC dollars allowed, reflecting the substantial capital and payroll outlays of mid-sized and large corporate claimants. Simultaneously, refundable credits accounted for 59.0% of all SR&ED credits allowed in 2025/26 (up from 57.0% in 2022/23 and 2023/24), demonstrating the critical role of cash-back tax credits in financing pre-profit and scaling enterprises. Sectorally, software development absorbed 42.6% of all SR&ED tax credits allowed in 2025/26—representing approximately $1.96 billion, up roughly 66% from $1.18 billion in 2021/22—whereas all other scientific and technological disciplines combined grew by approximately 24% over the same period. This disproportionate expansion in software claims has prompted heightened CRA audit scrutiny regarding the statutory boundary between routine software engineering and genuine experimental development under subsection 248(1) of the ITA.
The 2024–2026 Legislative Overhaul and Enactment of Bill C-15
Policy Genesis and Consultation Trajectory

The modernization of the federal SR&ED regime began formally on January 31, 2024, when the Department of Finance Canada launched Phase 1 of its public consultation on the SR&ED program, which ran until April 15, 2024. Originally framed as a review of cost-neutral improvements, the consultation sought stakeholder input on seven core architectural questions: maintaining effectiveness across business sizes, supporting R&D-intensive scale-ups, refining the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1), improving complementarity with direct funding platforms (such as the Industrial Research Assistance Program [IRAP], the Strategic Innovation Fund, the Regional Development Agencies, and the Trade Commissioner Service), targeting assistance more effectively, ensuring domestic retention of intellectual property (IP) alongside a parallel patent box consultation, and streamlining administrative access for entrepreneurs.

On April 16, 2024, the federal government tabled Budget 2024: Fairness for Every Generation, shifting from a strictly cost-neutral posture to a net fiscal expansion by committing $600 million over four years beginning in 2025, with $150 million per year in ongoing funding, to enhance the SR&ED program. Budget 2024 also launched a second phase of technical consultations that remained open until May 27, 2024, focusing specifically on technical eligibility reforms, restoration of capital expenditures, and extending the 35% enhanced ITC rate to Canadian public companies. Following interim policy announcements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (which initially proposed raising the expenditure limit to $4.5 million) and further expansion in the federal budget tabled on November 4, 2025, the federal government tabled Bill C-15 in Parliament on November 18, 2025. Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, codifying the enhanced SR&ED parameters into the Income Tax Act with retroactive application to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024).
The Two-Tier Federal ITC Rate Structure and Bill C-15 Enhancements

Under section 127 of the ITA, the federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier investment tax credit architecture that distinguishes between qualifying domestic corporations and other claimants. The first tier is the Enhanced 35% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit, which is available to qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. Under Bill C-15, the maximum annual expenditure limit doubled from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, which must be allocated across an associated corporate group. Consequently, the maximum annual refundable federal ITC at the 35% rate doubled from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. For qualifying corporations that are not excluded corporations, the 35% ITC earned on current expenditures (and, post-December 15, 2024, 40% of the credit earned on capital expenditures where applicable under subsection 127.1(1)) is 100% refundable on current SR&ED expenditures up to the expenditure limit, providing non-dilutive cash flow even when the corporation has zero federal income tax payable.

The second tier is the Basic 15% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit, which applies to foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, individuals (sole proprietors), trusts, partnerships, and qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs that exceed their annual $6.0 million expenditure limit. For corporations that are not qualifying CCPCs or ECPCs, the 15% basic ITC is strictly non-refundable and may only be applied to offset federal Part I tax otherwise payable. For qualifying CCPCs whose current SR&ED expenditures exceed their annual expenditure limit, the 15% ITC earned on excess current expenditures is 40% refundable, yielding a 6.0% effective cash refund rate on excess spending. Any unused non-refundable SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years and carried forward 20 taxation years under subsection 127(9) of the ITA.

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

Whereas the 2019 Federal Budget repealed the prior-year taxable income phase-out (which previously reduced the expenditure limit when prior-year taxable income of the associated group fell between $500,000 and $800,000 for taxation years ending on or before March 18, 2019), the expenditure limit remains subject to a phase-out based on the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the claimant and its associated corporations. Under the enacted Bill C-15 provisions for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the $6.0 million base expenditure limit begins to phase out linearly when aggregate prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15.0 million and is fully extinguished at $75.0 million.

If the corporation's current taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks (357 days), the calculated expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365.

A critical structural innovation enacted in Bill C-15 is the interplay between the extension of the 35% credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the introduction of an elective gross revenue phase-out for CCPCs. Because public corporations frequently carry substantial share capital and retained earnings on their balance sheets—which inflates Part I.3 taxable capital even among mid-sized, R&D-intensive public technology and biotechnology enterprises—the ECPC expenditure limit phase-out is governed by a three-year average gross revenue threshold rather than taxable capital. Recognizing that venture-backed private scale-ups (CCPCs) that have raised large equity financing rounds also accumulate significant taxable capital long before achieving commercial scale, Bill C-15 permits CCPCs and their associated groups to formally elect to have their $6.0 million expenditure limit phased out using the three-year average revenue formula applicable to ECPCs instead of the $15 million to $75 million taxable capital test. Tax advisors and corporate controllers must therefore model both the Part I.3 taxable capital calculation and the three-year consolidated gross revenue average across all associated entities prior to filing Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31.
Statutory Definition of Eligible SR&ED Work Under Subsection 248(1)

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls into one of three core categories, supplemented by directly commensurate support work. First, paragraph 248(1)(a) encompasses basic research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Second, paragraph 248(1)(b) covers applied research, namely work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Third, paragraph 248(1)(c) governs experimental development, which is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Over 95% of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under the experimental development branch. Finally, paragraph 248(1)(d) incorporates eligible support work, defined as work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity from qualifying as SR&ED. Specifically, paragraph 248(1)(e) excludes market research or sales promotion; paragraph 248(1)(f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; paragraph 248(1)(g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities; paragraph 248(1)(h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; paragraph 248(1)(i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; paragraph 248(1)(j) excludes style changes; and paragraph 248(1)(k) excludes routine data collection.

In administering subsection 248(1), the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (which replaced Information Circular IC 86-4R3 and subsequent sector-specific policies on December 19, 2012, and were updated through 2026) evaluate every claimed project across two foundational pillars: why the work was conducted (to achieve a scientific or technological advancement by resolving an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty) and how the work was conducted (through a systematic investigation or search involving hypothesis formulation, testing by experiment or analysis, and logical conclusions documented contemporaneously). As confirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77, while CRA administrative guidelines provide a useful analytical framework, in the event of any conflict between CRA policy documents and the Income Tax Act, the statutory text of subsection 248(1) strictly governs.

An "SR&ED project" is defined by the CRA at the level required to recognize all interrelated activities collectively necessary to resolve a defined scientific or technological uncertainty. Crucially, once the scientific or technological uncertainty is resolved, or once the claimant determines that the uncertainty cannot be resolved, or terminates the project, the eligibility of the work ceases immediately. In software development—which captured 42.6% of all allowed SR&ED credits in 2025/26—routine coding, standard system integration, debugging using established tools, API wrapping, or overcoming commercial or project-management complexity does not qualify as SR&ED unless the team confronts a genuine system-level or algorithmic technological uncertainty where standard computer science knowledge and publicly available documentation cannot predict whether or how the target architectural state can be achieved.
Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Elections, and Capital Cost Restoration
Allowable Current Expenditures and Specified Employee Restrictions

Once an SR&ED project satisfies subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its Allowable SR&ED Expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661, deduct non-qualifying amounts and assistance to establish its Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (section 37) and Qualified SR&ED Expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 (section 127), and compute the resulting ITC on Schedule T2SCH31. Eligible expenditure categories are strictly governed by section 37 of the ITA and Regulation 2900.
Salaries and Wages (Lines 300 to 309 of Form T661)

Only salaries and wages of employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (plus a limited allowance under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) for permissible SR&ED wages incurred outside Canada, capped at 10% of total SR&ED salaries and wages paid to Canadian-resident employees for work performed in Canada) may be included in the direct labour base. Eligible remuneration includes gross base salary, regular wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, and employer contributions to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and provincial workers' compensation boards, provided the amounts are incurred in the taxation year and paid no later than 180 days after the end of the taxation year under subsection 78(4) of the ITA.

Strict statutory anti-avoidance restrictions apply to specified employees—defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who are "specified shareholders" (holding, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who do not deal at arm's length with the employer. For direct SR&ED salary claims (Line 305), a specified employee's eligible remuneration cannot include any bonus or remuneration based on profits, and the maximum direct salary claimable is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year the individual is a specified employee.

Furthermore, when calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the proxy overhead method, Regulation 2900(7) imposes a much tighter ceiling on a specified employee's salary included in the proxy salary base (Part 5 of Form T661): the inclusion is capped at the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages for the year (before applying the SR&ED time allocation percentage) and 2.5 × YMPE, prorated by the number of days employed in the year divided by 365:
Proxy base cap = lesser of [75% × total salary and wages] and [2.5 × YMPE] × (days employed in the year ÷ 365)

Under Regulation 2900(8), if the same specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the maximum 2.5 × YMPE ceiling must be allocated among the associated corporations using an agreement filed in prescribed form, preventing multiplication of the proxy base cap across related corporate payrolls. With the YMPE rising from $68,500 in 2024 to $71,300 in 2025 and $74,600 in 2026, the 2.5 × YMPE proxy base cap corresponds to $171,250 for 2024, $178,250 for 2025, and $186,500 for 2026.
Materials Consumed or Transformed (Lines 320 and 325 of Form T661)

Claimants may include the cost of materials that are either materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED (rendered virtually worthless or destroyed through experimental testing, reported on Line 320) or materials transformed into another product or prototype during SR&ED (reported on Line 325). However, if materials transformed—or experimental prototypes, pilot plants, or custom-built assets containing SR&ED materials—are subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use in the claimant's business, the SR&ED recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to 127(35) of the ITA are triggered. Under recapture, the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value at the time of conversion to commercial use) and the original cost claimed as SR&ED is multiplied by the ITC rate originally earned on the property and added directly back to the taxpayer's federal Part I tax payable in the year of sale or conversion.
Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments (Lines 340, 345, and 370 of Form T661)

For SR&ED performed in Canada on behalf of the claimant by an arm's-length contractor (Line 340), the claimant may include the contract expenditure in its section 37 deduction pool in full, but pursuant to subsection 127(9) of the ITA, only 80% of the eligible arm's-length contract payment qualifies as a "qualified expenditure" for computing the section 127 ITC (a statutory disallowance designed to strip out the contractor's assumed commercial profit margin and non-qualifying overhead). Conversely, for non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts (Line 345), the payor earns 0% ITC directly on payments made to a non-arm's-length performer; instead, the non-arm's-length performer must incur the underlying SR&ED expenditures and the parties may execute Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(13) to transfer the qualified expenditures (up to the contract amount, reported on Line 540 by the performer and Line 508 by the transferee) to the payor. Similarly, where non-arm's-length parties share government or non-government assistance, they must file Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026). Third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations (Line 370) are likewise subject to the 80% ITC inclusion rule.
Proxy Method Versus Traditional Overhead Method

A claimant must make an irrevocable annual election on Form T661 for each taxation year between two mutually exclusive methods for capturing SR&ED overhead expenditures. The first option is the Prescribed Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 of Form T661), which is selected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants due to its administrative simplicity and high yield for labour-intensive R&D. When electing Line 160, the claimant enters "0" on Line 360 (claiming no specific SR&ED overhead) and completes Part 5 of Form T661 to compute the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on Line 502. Under Regulation 2900(4), the PPA is equal to 55% of the total eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (subject to the Regulation 2900(7) cap for specified employees and an overall ceiling under Regulation 2900(6) preventing the salary base from exceeding total business salaries net of specific deductions). Because the PPA is a notional calculation, it is not deducted in computing net income for tax purposes and does not enter the section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool; however, the PPA is added directly to qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 502 of Part 4 to earn federal and applicable provincial SR&ED investment tax credits.

The second option is the Traditional Method (elected by ticking Line 162 of Form T661), under which the claimant omits Part 5, enters "0" on Lines 355 and 502, and itemizes actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360. To qualify on Line 360 under subsection 37(1) and Regulation 2900(2)(c), overhead costs must be directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, such as the incremental portion of shop supplies, utilities, clerical support, or maintenance directly tied to an R&D facility. Under the post-Bill C-15 rules, claimants electing the Traditional Method may also claim on Line 360 the SR&ED portion of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% (all or substantially all) of the time, provided the equipment is used more than 50% in SR&ED or the incremental lease cost is directly attributable.
Restoration of SR&ED Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, all capital expenditures (and payments for the right to use or lease property that would be capital if owned) were excluded from SR&ED eligibility. Bill C-15 repealed this 11-year exclusion for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). The CRA's updated Form T661 (May 2026 version) and technical guidance establish rigorous rules for post-December 15, 2024 capital claims across wholly dedicated assets, shared-use machinery, and leased equipment.

For All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property reported on Line 390 of Form T661, new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, that is intended to be used all or substantially all (≥90% of its operating time over its useful life) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualifies both for immediate inclusion in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (where Line 400 equals the sum of Line 380 current expenditures and Line 390 capital expenditures) and for the section 127 SR&ED ITC. Non-depreciable assets such as land and buildings (including leasehold interests in buildings) remain strictly excluded from SR&ED capital eligibility.

Where a claimant acquires new depreciable machinery or equipment after December 15, 2024, that is used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time, its cost does not enter the section 37 deductible SR&ED pool on Line 390; instead, its capital cost must be depreciated under standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) classes on Schedule T2SCH8. However, if the new equipment is used primarily (>50% of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during its operational assembly and testing phases, it qualifies as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 for ITC purposes under both the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method. Specifically, on Line 504, the claimant may claim First-Term SUE equal to 25% of the capital cost of the equipment if it is used >50% in SR&ED during the first period (extending from the time the property becomes available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time), and Second-Term SUE equal to an additional 25% of the capital cost (totalling 50% across both periods) if the equipment continues to be used >50% in SR&ED through the end of the second period (the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after the property became available for use). Furthermore, on Form T661, claimants must explicitly schedule and identify the 20 most expensive shared-use equipment properties acquired after December 15, 2024.

With respect to leased equipment, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used ASA (≥90%) in SR&ED qualify under both the Proxy Method (where 50% of the lease cost of general-purpose electronic data processing equipment or 100% of specialized SR&ED equipment lease costs apply under statutory formulas) and the Traditional Method, whereas lease costs for equipment used <90% in SR&ED may be claimed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method. In all cases (including Line 535 and Line 540 non-arm's-length transfers), expenditures for depreciable property or lease rights acquired before December 16, 2024, remain strictly ineligible.
Complementary Immediate Expensing and Accelerated CCA Measures

Beyond the section 37 and section 127 SR&ED capital restoration, Bill C-15 enacted two major Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) incentives on Schedule T2SCH8 that directly benefit R&D-performing enterprises. First, Bill C-15 provides 100% immediate expensing for qualifying purchases of property acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027, across three critical innovation asset classes: CCA Class 44 (normally 25% declining balance), covering patents or a right to use patented information for a limited or unlimited period; CCA Class 46 (normally 30%), covering data network infrastructure equipment and related systems software; and CCA Class 50 (normally 55%), covering general-purpose electronic data-processing equipment (computers, servers, and GPUs) and systems software. Second, Bill C-15 temporarily reinstated the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII) and immediate expensing for qualifying assets acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, with a gradual phase-out between 2030 and 2033 replacing the prior 2024–2027 phase-out schedule. In addition, tax practitioners are monitoring the federal government's proposed "Productivity Mega Deduction" announced in late 2025 and 2026 to allow immediate write-offs across a broader range of capital investments.

body.text: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentives and Structural Reforms

Almost every Canadian province and territory supplements the federal SR&ED program with jurisdiction-specific R&D tax credits or grants. Except for Quebec (administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered independently by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA]), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA under federal-provincial tax collection agreements and are claimed on specialized schedules attached to the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return.
Quebec: The March 25, 2025 Abolition of Legacy Credits and Launch of CRIC

Quebec has historically maintained the most complex suite of provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada, administered by Revenu Québec under the Taxation Act (Quebec). However, in its 2025–2026 Budget tabled on March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a sweeping structural consolidation that fundamentally altered provincial R&D funding for fiscal periods and taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.

For any corporation or qualified partnership whose taxation year or fiscal period begins after March 25, 2025, Revenu Québec eliminated five longstanding R&D and technology tax credits alongside the elimination of industrial design tax credits. The abolished incentives comprise the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.7, with associated group expenditure limit allocations on Form RD-1029.7.8, which previously offered refundable rates ranging from a 14% basic rate up to a 30% enhanced rate—and 17.5% to 37.5% prior to June 5, 2014—on up to $3.0 million of eligible R&D salaries and 50% of arm's-length subcontractor payments above an asset-scaled exclusion threshold); the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.8.6, providing 14% to 35% refundable credits); the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (formerly claimed on Form RD-1029.8.16.1, providing 14% to 35% refundable credits); the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (subject to transitional rules governing a claimant's existing eligible fee balance); and the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services.

To replace these fragmented legacy credits for taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec introduced the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation). Unlike the legacy RD-1029.7 regime—which was strictly limited to R&D salaries and subcontractor labour—the new CRIC regime covers both R&D activities and pre-commercialization activities (such as regulatory compliance testing, industrial design, pilot validation, and technological adaptation aimed at bringing an R&D innovation to market) carried out in Quebec. Qualifying expenditures under CRIC explicitly encompass four pillars: salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to eligible research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec, thereby aligning Quebec's provincial base with the federal Bill C-15 capital restoration.

The CRIC provides a fully refundable 30% enhanced tax credit rate on the first $1.0 million of eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold for all corporations (regardless of asset size or public/private status), and a 20% standard refundable rate on eligible expenditures exceeding that tier. Rather than scaling the exclusion threshold by corporate assets, the CRIC exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 and the sum of the per-employee thresholds, calculated by multiplying the Quebec basic personal income tax amount ($18,571 for 2025) by the number of full-time equivalent employees dedicating time to R&D and pre-commercialization activities; for example, an enterprise with 10 full-time R&D employees has an exclusion threshold of $185,710 (10 × $18,571), and only eligible expenditures exceeding $185,710 earn the CRIC credit.
Ontario: The Three-Tier CRA-Administered Credit System

Corporations maintaining a permanent establishment in Ontario and conducting qualifying SR&ED within the province may stack up to three distinct provincial tax credits administered by the CRA under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario). First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (T2SCH566), is a fully refundable 8% tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016) available to CCPCs on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit of $3.0 million, yielding a maximum refundable credit of $240,000 per year. Unlike the federal expenditure limit, which doubled to $6.0 million under Bill C-15, the Ontario OITC expenditure cap remains fixed at $3.0 million and phases out when the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25 million and $50 million, or when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000. Under Ontario's harmonized base rules, 100% of direct Ontario SR&ED wages, 100% of materials, the 55% federal PPA (or traditional overhead), 80% of arm's-length Ontario subcontractor payments, and restored post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures qualify.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508 (T2SCH508), is a non-refundable 3.5% tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for taxation years commencing after May 31, 2016) available to all corporations (including CCPCs, public corporations, and foreign-controlled subsidiaries) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario, with no expenditure limit. When a CCPC claims both the 8% OITC and the 3.5% ORDTC on the same expenditure base, the OITC is treated as government assistance that reduces the qualified expenditure pool for ORDTC purposes (unless the corporation elects on Schedule 566 or Schedule 508 to waive the credit to prevent grinding the federal pool), and unused ORDTC balances may be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedule 568 alongside a separate Schedule 569 for each eligible contract, provides a fully refundable 20% tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an approved Ontario research institute (such as an Ontario university, college of applied arts and technology, or hospital research institute), subject to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20.0 million ($4.0 million maximum annual refund).
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Following the elimination of Alberta's legacy 10% SR&ED tax credit (formerly AB Schedule 9) effective January 1, 2020, the Government of Alberta enacted the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) effective January 1, 2021, under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act. Administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) and claimed by filing Form AT1 Schedule 29 (AT29) and the AT1 Schedule 29 Listing within 18 months of the end of the taxation year, the IEG is a fully refundable two-tier incentive designed to reward both base R&D activity and incremental R&D growth in Alberta.

Under the Part I Calculation on Line 110 of Form AT29, the corporation earns an 8% base refundable grant on the lesser of its eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures (Line 031) and its maximum expenditure limit for the year (Line 108). Under the Part II Calculation, the corporation earns an additional 12% incremental refundable grant—bringing the combined marginal rate to 20%—on the portion of current-year eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures that exceeds the corporation's base spending amount, which is defined as the average of the corporation's eligible Alberta SR&ED expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years (reported on Line 290 and related lines of Form AT29). The maximum annual expenditure limit for the IEG is $4.0 million (Line 108 and Line 208), which must be shared among associated corporations (allocated in Column 240 and Line 270 of Form AT29). Unlike the federal SR&ED limit, the Alberta IEG is available to all corporations (private, public, or foreign-controlled) that maintain a permanent establishment in Alberta, subject to a phase-out of the $4.0 million expenditure limit when the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (Line 300) is between $10.0 million and $50.0 million. In computing eligible Alberta expenditures on Line 031, the Alberta proxy amount (Line 009) is equal to 55% of the federal proxy salary base paid in respect of SR&ED carried out in Alberta.
British Columbia, Prairie, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

Across Western Canada, the Atlantic region, and the territories, the CRA administers several specialized R&D tax credit statutes. The British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit (claimed on Form T666 under Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act) applies to qualifying SR&ED carried out in British Columbia; the Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026 (S.B.C. 2026, c. 5) removed the former sunset date of September 1, 2027, making the credit permanent. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 10% fully refundable tax credit on qualified B.C. SR&ED expenditures up to their annual $6.0 million expenditure limit (maximum $600,000 cash refund), while other corporations and CCPCs or ECPCs with expenditures exceeding the $6.0 million limit earn a 10% non-refundable tax credit that can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years. In Saskatchewan, the R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 403) provides a 10% refundable tax credit for CCPCs on the first $1.0 million of qualifying Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures, and a 10% non-refundable tax credit for non-CCPCs and CCPC expenditures above $1.0 million, up to a combined annual credit cap of $1.0 million ($10.0 million in qualified expenditures), with a 3-year carryback and 10-year carryforward.

In Manitoba, the R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 380) provides a 15% tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the province. One-half of the Manitoba credit (7.5% effective rate) is refundable for corporations performing in-house R&D, while the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback); however, if the R&D is performed in Manitoba under contract with a qualifying educational or research institution, the entire 15% credit is fully refundable. In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit to all corporations (both CCPCs and non-CCPCs) with no expenditure limit, whereas Prince Edward Island relies on direct Innovation PEI grants rather than a statutory corporate tax credit. Finally, the Yukon R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 442) provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in the territory, plus an additional 5% refundable supplement (yielding a 20% total rate) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University (formerly Yukon College).

body.text: Interaction With Direct Government Grants, Clean Economy ITCs, and Stacking Mechanics
Direct Federal Innovation Funding Platforms

As outlined by the Department of Finance Canada during the 2024–2025 SR&ED policy review, Canadian businesses routinely combine statutory SR&ED tax credits with direct, non-dilutive federal funding delivered across four primary institutional platforms. The foremost SME platform is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides direct cost-shared wage subsidies (typically covering 50% to 80% of internal R&D technical salaries and contractor fees) and advisory services through Industrial Technology Advisors to innovative Canadian SMEs, bolstered in Budget 2024 by a dedicated $100 million allocation for the NRC AI Assist Program to help SMEs build and deploy artificial intelligence solutions. The second platform is the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED), which provides large-scale repayable and non-repayable contributions targeting industrial R&D commercialization, scale-up manufacturing, and net-zero industrial transformation. The third platform comprises Canada's Regional Development Agencies (RDAs), which deliver regionally tailored R&D and commercialization grants and zero-interest repayable contributions, reinforced by $200 million in Budget 2024 to accelerate AI adoption and startup commercialization across key industrial sectors. The fourth platform is the Trade Commissioner Service (TCS), operated by Global Affairs Canada, which facilitates international R&D commercialization and technology partnerships.

In addition to these four core platforms, the federal government deployed a $2.4 billion Artificial Intelligence package in Budget 2024, anchored by $2.0 billion for the AI Compute Access Fund and the Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy to subsidize high-performance computing infrastructure for domestic R&D teams, alongside ongoing funding under the $2.0 billion Global Innovation Clusters program, $50 million for workforce transition in AI-impacted sectors, and $14.5 million over two years for ISED's Innovation Asset Collective (IAC) to strengthen SME patent creation and IP retention. Furthermore, Bill C-15 enacted and expanded the Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits—including the Clean Technology ITC (providing up to a 30% refundable credit on clean energy generation and storage capital property in CCA Classes 43.1 and 43.2), the Clean Electricity ITC (implemented by Bill C-15 and expanded to include the Canada Infrastructure Bank and Canada Growth Fund), and related clean manufacturing incentives.
Statutory Grind-Down Rules for Government Assistance and Stacking Calculations

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) and 127(18) to 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant cannot earn a federal SR&ED investment tax credit on the portion of an expenditure that has already been funded, or is entitled to be funded, by government assistance or non-government assistance. "Government assistance" is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance—other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Consequently, both direct grants (such as NRC IRAP reimbursements) and provincial or territorial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario OITC and ORDTC, the Quebec CRIC, the B.C. SR&ED credit, and the Alberta IEG) constitute government assistance that reduces ("grinds down") the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool on Line 515 of Form T661 dollar-for-dollar before the federal 35% or 15% ITC is computed. Furthermore, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, the federal SR&ED ITCs deducted in a taxation year reduce the section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year, whereas provincial R&D tax credits, as government assistance, reduce the pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) for the year in which the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive or can reasonably be expected to receive them.

Importantly, when stacking a direct wage grant (such as NRC IRAP) with SR&ED under the Prescribed Proxy Method, a powerful mathematical leverage effect occurs—commonly referred to in Canadian R&D tax practice as the "Proxy Shield". Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed in Part 5 of Form T661 on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before government assistance is deducted in Part 4 (Line 515), an IRAP grant covering, for example, 80% of an employee's direct R&D salary reduces the direct salary in Part 4 by 80%, but leaves the entire 55% PPA intact to earn federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits.

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of provincial-federal credit grinding (without an external grant), consider a qualifying CCPC incurring $100,000 of direct, in-house SR&ED engineering salaries in 2025/2026 under the Proxy Method (55% PPA = $55,000; Total Qualified Expenditure Pool before assistance = $155,000):

body.text: Administrative Filing Procedures, CRA Audit Architecture, and Preparer Penalties
Mandatory Prescribed Forms and the Absolute 18-Month Reporting Deadline

To access federal SR&ED deductions and investment tax credits, a claimant must submit a complete package of prescribed forms with its income tax return for the year. Specifically, the filing package requires Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, updated May 15 and May 22, 2026, completed in accordance with Guide T4088) together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) for sole proprietorships and trusts. Where applicable, claimants must also file Form T1145 (allocation of assistance among non-arm's-length parties, updated May 15, 2026), Form T1146 (transfer of qualified expenditures under non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts, updated May 15, 2026), Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA schedule for shared-use equipment and accelerated CCA classes), and the relevant provincial schedules attached to the T2 return (such as Ontario Schedules 508, 566, 568, and 569, or B.C. Form T666), alongside standalone provincial filings for Revenu Québec and Alberta TRA (Form AT1 Schedule 29).

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the year. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporate claimant has an absolute statutory deadline of exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing all prescribed information.

The 18-month reporting deadline is a rigid statutory bar: the Minister of National Revenue has no discretionary authority under the fairness or taxpayer relief provisions of the ITA to extend the 18-month deadline or waive the requirement to file prescribed information on time. If a claimant omits a required project description field in Section B of Part 2 of Form T661 (unless the project is formally designated as "classified information" for national security reasons by a federal agency, in which case Section B of Part 2 is retained on a separate sheet in the claimant's records while a copy of the agency's classification letter is submitted with Form T661) or fails to list specific expenditure lines on Form T661 before the 18-month deadline expires, those expenditures are permanently disallowed as SR&ED.
CRA Internal Processing Systems, Audit Selection, and the April 1, 2026 Pre-Claim Approval Process

When an SR&ED claim is transmitted electronically (or filed on paper on top of the return where commercial software is not used), the data from Form T661 is ingested into the CRA's CORTAX corporate tax processing system. SR&ED field specialists access CORTAX to extract Form T661 data and conduct risk assessments, recording all technical and financial audit actions inside the AIMS (Audit Information Management System) database, whereas T1 unincorporated SR&ED claims have been stored in Integras since May 2019, with Social Insurance Numbers collected and verified pursuant to section 237 of the ITA.

During initial workload selection, the CRA's automated risk-scoring engine and initial technical screeners evaluate the clarity and technical specificity of the project narratives in Section B of Part 2 of Form T661. Section B of Part 2 imposes strict word limits across three core technical disclosures: Line 242 requires the claimant to identify the scientific or technological uncertainties that the project attempted to overcome (maximum 350 words); Line 244 requires a chronological technical description of the systematic work, hypotheses, experiments, and analyses performed in the taxation year to overcome the uncertainties described on Line 242 (maximum 700 words); and Line 246 requires a description of the scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted as a result of the work described on Line 244 (maximum 350 words).

As documented in the CRA's 2025/26 program statistics, 90.0% of processed SR&ED claims were accepted as filed, 6.0% were accepted after modifications, and 4.0% were denied in full. For claims accepted as filed during initial workload selection, the CRA processed 95.0% within 60 calendar days. If a claim is selected for a detailed field review, the CRA assigns a dual examination team comprising a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA)—a domain specialist with an engineering or scientific background who evaluates whether the claimed projects satisfy subsection 248(1) and may consult a National Technology Sector Specialist in complex cases—and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who audits payroll ledgers, T4 summaries, time-tracking records, subcontractor contracts, and proof of payment.

To reduce working-capital uncertainty for innovative businesses, effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a new Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process. Under this program, claimants can submit their technical project eligibility for upfront CRA validation prior to or alongside their fiscal filing; for claims that complete this elective pre-claim approval pathway and subsequently require an expenditure review, the CRA's processing timeline is cut in half from 180 days to 90 days.
Claim Preparer Disclosure Mandate and Subsection 162(5.1) Penalties

Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim preparer information) requires mandatory disclosure of every external consultant, accounting firm, or advisor ("claim preparer") that has accepted or agreed to accept consideration to prepare or assist in the preparation of the SR&ED claim. Specifically, Part 9 requires the preparer's business number, name, billing arrangement code (distinguishing between contingency fee arrangements, flat fees, hourly rates, or hybrid structures), billing rate or percentage, and total fee paid or payable. Even if no external claim preparer assisted in preparing Form T661, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9 to certify that the claim was prepared entirely in-house. If multiple claim preparers assisted on different projects, a separate Form T661 containing Part 9 must be completed for each preparer.

Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if any required prescribed claim preparer information in Part 9 of Form T661 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a statutory penalty of $1,000 may be assessed. Crucially, the claimant corporation and the external claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable for paying the $1,000 penalty unless the claim preparer exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill to prevent the omission that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances.
Judicial Precedents and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

Because subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED through principles-based scientific and technological criteria rather than industry checklists, Canadian SR&ED audit defence is governed heavily by jurisprudence from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court (FC), and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants and C.W. Agencies

The bedrock precedent of Canadian SR&ED law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CarswellNat 696, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), written by Judge Donald Bowman. Dealing with complex physical scale modelling of hydraulic structures, Judge Bowman distilled the statutory requirements of subsection 248(1) into a five-criteria judicial test that remains the standard applied in every Tax Court appeal. First, the court asks whether there was a technical risk or technological uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures known to competent professionals in the field. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the systematic formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through experiment or analysis. Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—that is to say, an advancement in the general understanding of technology—establishing that technical or commercial failure still qualifies as a technological advancement where systematic experimentation proves that a plausible hypothesis does not work. Fifth, the court assesses whether the taxpayer kept a detailed, contemporaneous record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, the Federal Court of Appeal elevated Judge Bowman's Northwest Hydraulic framework to binding appellate authority across Canada, confirming that development expenses qualify as SR&ED only where there is genuine technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved by resorting to current knowledge or studies, coupled with systematic research work directly aimed at resolving that uncertainty.
Software Engineering, Routine Development, and Contemporaneous Time-Tracking Precedents

As software claims expanded to 42.6% of all allowed SR&ED credits by 2025/26, the Tax Court of Canada issued a series of strict rulings delineating the boundary between standard software programming and eligible SR&ED, as well as the evidentiary burden for proving employee hours. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 65, 2015 DTC 1089, the corporate taxpayer provided computer software services and claimed SR&ED ITCs for its 2012 taxation year regarding the development of a software program capable of inspecting and verifying websites. While the Minister of National Revenue permitted the deduction of the software expenses as ordinary business expenses, the Minister disallowed the SR&ED characterization. Dismissing the taxpayer's appeal, the Tax Court applied C.W. Agencies Inc. and held that the claimant's programming activities constituted nothing more than normal analyses carried out by competent programmers using current technology and standard techniques, rather than overcoming genuine technological uncertainty. Furthermore, at paragraph 48 of Hypercube, the Court established a strict evidentiary rule: an accurate record of hours worked must be provided to substantiate an SR&ED salary claim.

Subsequently, in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 32, the Tax Court reaffirmed and applied Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (at para 48) to dismiss a claimant's appeal where the corporation failed to maintain exact details and contemporaneous time sheets of the hours spent by employees on the claimed SR&ED projects. The Court noted that retroactive, reconstructed percentage estimates of employee time, paired with vague and insufficiently detailed descriptions of the technical tasks performed by each employee, cannot satisfy the taxpayer's burden of proof. Similarly, in Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, and Imapro Corporation v. The Queen, 92 DTC 1487 (TCC), the Tax Court underscored that while genuine software-hardware systems experimentation qualifies, relying on uncorroborated oral testimony without documentary proof of systematic hypothesis testing leads to dismissal.
Post-Commercial Release Experimentation and Statutory Primacy: 6379249 Canada Inc.

In 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77 (Docket 2012-3634(IT)G), the Tax Court of Canada addressed a critical recurring audit dispute: whether experimental development conducted on a hardware product after initial units have been released commercially can still qualify as SR&ED under subsection 248(1). The appellant developed an ultra-compact portable printer; while the CRA's National Technology Sector Specialist (Mr. Wierzbica) accepted the 2006 and 2007 taxation years as eligible SR&ED because no publicly available technical guidance existed on building such a miniature printing device, the CRA disallowed the 2009 and 2010 claims primarily because the printer had already been sent to manufacturing and commercially released.

During the hearing, the evidence established that under longer-term dynamic operation in 2009 and 2010, the portable printer failed to consistently meet specifications due to motor stalling caused by power consumption imbalances between static and dynamic mechanical regimes. The appellant opened a new SR&ED investigation and conducted systematic experimental tests using specialized felt configurations to balance the motor's power consumption across static and dynamic regimes and minimize stalling frequency. Notably, the CRA's own specialist conceded on cross-examination that had the product not been commercially released, the 2009 and 2010 continuation work would likely have been accepted as resolving unresolved technological uncertainty. The Tax Court allowed the appeal, holding that the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the ITA—not rigid administrative assumptions regarding commercial release—governs eligibility, and that systematic experimental development undertaken to resolve persistent technological uncertainties in an existing commercial product qualifies for SR&ED tax credits.
Strict Enforcement of the 18-Month Prescribed Information Deadline: AFD Petroleum Ltd.

In AFD Petroleum Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2016 FC 547 (Docket T-309-15), the Federal Court confirmed that submitting an incomplete Form T661 on the 18-month filing deadline is fatal to an SR&ED claim. The applicant, an Alberta-based fuel and lubricant supplier, sought to amend its 2012 corporate income tax return on the final statutory filing date (December 31, 2013) to claim approximately $357,000 in SR&ED expenditures incurred to develop a portable refuelling mechanism for hydraulic fracturing (fracking) equipment. However, when the claim was transmitted on the deadline, the CRA received only two of the seven pages that then comprised Part 2 of Form T661, omitting the mandatory responses to Lines 242 and 244.

On January 22, 2014, and again on January 30, 2015, the CRA rejected the SR&ED claim as incomplete because all prescribed information required by Part 2 of Form T661 had not been filed within 12 months after the T2 filing due date. The applicant applied for judicial review under section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, arguing that the submitted pages (specifically Line 240) holistically contained the substance of the required information. Dismissing the application, Justice Boswell held that the CRA lawfully refused to accept the claim: because the applicant failed to supply the specific prescribed information mandated at Lines 242 and 244 of Form T661 prior to the expiration of the statutory 18-month deadline, the claim was statutorily invalid.

body.text: Strategic Audit Governance and Compliance Conclusions

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside Quebec's transition to the CRIC regime after March 25, 2025, and the CRA's launch of the elective pre-claim approval process on April 1, 2026, creates an exceptionally generous yet procedurally demanding R&D tax environment in Canada. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, corporate tax departments of scaling CCPCs with associated group taxable capital approaching or exceeding $15.0 million must model both the expanded $15.0 million to $75.0 million taxable capital phase-out and the new three-year average gross revenue phase-out election (borrowed from the ECPC rules) to preserve maximum access to the $6.0 million expenditure limit and the $2.1 million maximum refundable federal ITC. Concurrently, public Canadian technology, life sciences, and manufacturing corporations must restructure their tax provision workflows to transition from the 15% non-refundable credit to the 35% enhanced refundable ECPC credit.

At the operational level, engineering and fixed-asset accounting teams must tag all depreciable R&D machinery, testing rigs, and computing hardware acquired on or after December 16, 2024. Assets used ≥90% (ASA) in SR&ED should be routed to Line 390 of Form T661 for immediate section 37 deduction and 100% ITC inclusion, whereas assets used >50% but <90% in SR&ED must be tracked via operating-hour logs to substantiate First-Term (25%) and Second-Term (25%) Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) claims on Line 504 while simultaneously claiming 100% immediate CCA expensing on Schedule T2SCH8 if the assets fall within CCA Classes 44, 46, or 50 (acquired between April 16, 2024, and December 31, 2026). In parallel, corporations and partnerships operating establishments in Quebec with fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, must retire legacy RD-1029.7, RD-1029.8.6, and RD-1029.8.16.1 tracking templates and expand their internal cost capture to include pre-commercialization activities and capital property acquisitions eligible under the new 30% and 20% CRIC regime, while accurately computing the per-FTE exclusion threshold (the greater of $50,000 and $18,571 multiplied by full-time R&D personnel for 2025).

Finally, rigorous documentation and filing discipline remain the decisive factors in sustaining claims under audit. In light of the Tax Court of Canada's strict rulings in Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65 at para 48) and Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32), R&D-performing enterprises must integrate contemporaneous time-tracking directly into their project management and engineering repositories linked specifically to individual SR&ED technological uncertainties rather than commercial product features. In software development claims, technical narratives on Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661 must be drafted in the technical language of lead systems architects, isolating structural or algorithmic constraints from routine coding. Given the Federal Court's uncompromising enforcement of the 18-month prescribed information bar in AFD Petroleum Ltd. v. Canada (Attorney General) (2016 FC 547) and the $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under subsection 162(5.1) of the ITA, corporate controllers must verify that all pages of Part 2 and Part 9 of Form T661—along with Forms T1145 and T1146 for non-arm's-length groups—are fully populated and electronically confirmed well in advance of the 18-month deadline, while leveraging the CRA's April 1, 2026 Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process to compress expenditure review cycles from 180 days to 90 days.
